title: Titch and the Lost Lantern
markdown:
A little goblin named Titch lived high up in the Starfall Highlands, where stars sometimes fell like shiny soft stones after a gentle rain, and moonlight painted the hills in silver and deep blue. Titch was no bigger than a round mushroom by a mossy stone. Eyes as bright as shiny buttons, always looking, always wondering. A heart as soft and warm as the deepest moss cushion.

With him, always, was Pipkin: a very, very little mouse, whiskers twitching at the slightest new smell or sound, fur as soft as a fluffy seed ready to float. Pipkin loved Titch with all his tiny mouse heart, and Titch loved Pipkin just as much. Often Pipkin rode on Titch’s shoulder, little paws tucked neatly, or peeked from the leafy pocket of the tunic, pink nose wiggling.

One evening, as the moon, a great silver smile, stretched silvery fingers across the land, Titch remembered. “Oh, Pipkin, my dear little friend.” Gentle, so as not to startle. “I borrowed a lantern from old Farmer Giles. It shines with a light like a star, all warm and golden. I must take it back before the moon climbs too high and it’s too late.”

A determined nod. Little boots of the softest woven grass crunched the winding path down, down, down toward the edge of the Moonpetal Forest. Not a spooky forest. Trees with leaves like shiny silver, rustling with the slightest breath. Among the ferns, Moonpetals glowed like little fallen stars. Beneath the canopy Titch looked around with wide eyes. “Ooooh.” Pipkin squeaked in agreement, whiskers vibrating. Sweet clean dew, and something like warm honey mixed with sunshine.

He had meant to walk straight to Farmer Giles’s cozy cottage, lantern careful in both hands, because borrowed light is a kind of guest. But the forest was just so wonderfully pretty. He paused for a particularly large dewdrop on a silver leaf, sparkling like a tiny diamond, and then for another, because dewdrops, once you start, like to be counted. Then a little path of smooth moon-kissed pebbles led off the main way. “Just a little peek, Pipkin.” Already a step. Pipkin’s nose said yes, please, more wonder. The lantern bumped Titch’s knee, politely, as if it had opinions about peeks.

As they ambled, a sweet singing, like bees but much sweeter. Around a gentle bend, a sunny spot, a little hut, cheerful smoke of baked apples and fragrant herbs. Outside, tending a basket of interesting plants: a lady with the kindest smile Titch had ever seen, eyes twinkling like the stars. Agnes Crumble, a wise witch who knew the herbs of the Starfall Highlands.

“Well, hello there, little goblin!” Warm as steaming cocoa. “And who is this tiny whiskery friend?”

“This is Pipkin.” Titch held out his hand; Pipkin scampered on, tiny claws tickling. “And I am Titch. We were going to Farmer Giles’s to take back a lantern, but the forest is just so very pretty.”

Agnes chuckled, leaves rustling. “Ah, the Moonpetal Forest. It does have a way of making one forget the time.” Fingers stained with crushed petals. “For your journey back, take this sprig of Lumina-leaf. A very special shimmer. It helps you remember where you’re going, even on a moonlit night. It will help your thoughts stay clear.” A small feathery leaf, glowing, pulsing gently.

Titch held it, and truly remembered. “Oh dear! The lantern! Farmer Giles! I completely forgot!” Pipkin wiggled, sensing the worry.

Agnes’s knowing smile made him feel better at once. She did not compare promises to stars. She only nodded at the leaf, which was already doing the work.

He thanked her very, very much. Heart lighter. Lumina-leaf tucked in the leafy tunic, pulsing a friendly little nudge that said cottage, not pebble-path, which was not unkind, only clear. They hurried, boots quicker on the grass-weave, Pipkin holding tight. Moonpetals still glowed. Titch did not stop to count them. Soon, with a happy sigh, Farmer Giles, wonderfully bushy grey beard, was coming out of his door with a lantern-shaped worry already fading. Concern melted into a warm smile.

“Ah, Titch! I see you’ve brought my lantern back. Thank you, my boy. And hello to your little friend too!” A wink for Pipkin, whose whiskers twitched.

Titch handed over the lantern, a happy little sun in Farmer Giles’s hands. The grass-boots had dew on them still, proof of pebble-paths. Warmth spread: a promise kept. They waved, and Giles lifted the lantern once, as if to show the hills it was home. Home up the winding path to the Starfall Highlands, leaf still pulsing, not because he might forget again, but because it was a kind light to walk with.

Pipkin snuggled into Titch’s neck, a soft warm weight, smelling faintly of herbs and of apple smoke. The moon was high, a silver crescent, stars at their brightest. Titch was not worried. He had Pipkin, a warm home, and a lantern that now belonged where it had always belonged. Farmer Giles had not asked why they were late. He had only taken the light and winked, which was enough of a scolding for a pretty forest. The Lumina-leaf went in a cup on the sill, in case tomorrow’s forest was pretty too, which it would be.
characters: Titch (young goblin), Pipkin (mouse), Agnes Crumble (witch), Giles (farmer)
